// Read input
list($a, $b, $p, $x) = array_map('intval', explode(' ', trim(fgets(STDIN))));

// Fast power mod
function mod_pow($base, $exp, $mod) {

        $base = ($base * $base) % $mod;
        $exp >>= 1;
    }
    return $res;

// Extended GCD
function exgcd($a, $b, &$x, &$y) {
    if ($b == 0) {
        $x = 1; $y = 0;
        return $a;
    }
    $x1 = $y1 = 0;
    $g = exgcd($b, $a % $b, $x1, $y1);
    $x = $y1;
    $y = $x1 - intdiv($a, $b) * $y1;
    return $g;
}

// Modular inverse
function mod_inv($a, $mod) {
    $x = $y = 0;
    $g = exgcd($a, $mod, $x, $y);
    if ($g != 1) return -1;
    $x %= $mod;
    if ($x < 0) $x += $mod;
    return $x;
}

$mod = $p;
$phi = $p - 1;

// Precompute powers of a modulo p and their inverses modulo p

$invPowA = array_fill(0, $phi, 0);

    if ($log[$cur] == -1) $log[$cur] = $k;
    $cur = ($cur * $a) % $mod;

$ans = 0;

        // That means i ≡ k (mod p-1). Our construction ensures that.

        $base = ($base * $base) % $mod;

    $x = $y = 0;
    $g = exgcd($a, $mod, $x, $y);
    if ($g != 1) return -1;
    $x %= $mod;
    if ($x < 0) $x += $mod;
    return $x;
}

$phi = $p - 1;
$invA = mod_inv($a, $p);
$invAphi = mod_pow($invA, $phi, $p); // a^{p-1}^-1 mod p, but we'll use powers of invA

$powInvA = array_fill(0, $phi, 0);

    $powA[$k] = ($powA[$k-1] * $a) % $p;
    $powInvA[$k] = ($powInvA[$k-1] * $invA) % $p;

for ($k = 0; $k < $phi; $k++) {
    $v = $powA[$k];
    if ($pos[$v] == -1) $pos[$v] = $k;
}

$ans = 0;

// Iterate over i = n mod p
for ($i = 1; $i < $p; $i++) {
    $t = ($b * mod_inv($i, $p)) % $p; // t = b * inv(i) mod p
    $k = $pos[$t];

    // a^{n} = a^{i + p*t} = a^{i + t*(p mod (p-1))} mod p (Fermat)
    // But we already ensured a^k = t, so we solve k ≡ i + t*(p mod (p-1)) (mod p-1)
    // However, simpler known solution: n ≡ i (mod p) and n ≡ k (mod p-1)
    // Solve CRT for n0 in [0, p*(p-1))

    // Using standard CRT since p and p-1 are coprime
    $m1 = $p;
